title: Where it began and where it ended
lede: The chain reached 42 states at its height.[^1] We could not source a full list of locations, so this map shows only eight places we can document: where it started, how it first spread, and the last restaurants to close. All eight are in the Northeast.

figure.title: Howard Johnson’s: first and last locations, 1925–2022
figure.whatItShows: the origin in Quincy, the first franchise and the first turnpike contract, and the five last or best-known restaurants. Step through the timeline: sites appear when they opened and gray out when they closed.
figure.caption: Pins are placed at town level and nudged apart so they don’t overlap; a thin line joins a moved pin to its true location. Opening and closing dates known only to the year are placed on January 1 or mid-year for the animation; the text gives the precision the source gives. Base map: U.S. Census Bureau via us-atlas[^30].

pins.title: Quincy (Wollaston), Massachusetts
pins.text: The store Howard D. Johnson bought in 1925, and the first restaurant in 1929. Company headquarters stayed in Quincy.

pins.title: Orleans, Cape Cod
pins.text: The first franchised restaurant, 1935. Its closing date is not in our sources.

pins.title: Milford, Connecticut
pins.text: The first location outside Massachusetts, 1936. Our sources give no closing date.

pins.title: Pennsylvania Turnpike, Midway plaza (Bedford)
pins.text: One of 24 turnpike restaurants under the 1940 contract. The monopoly lasted until 1979.

pins.title: Lake George, New York
pins.text: Built 1953. Closed 2011, reopened January 2015, closed for good in spring 2022. The last one.

pins.title: Bangor, Maine
pins.text: Opened 1966 beside the motor lodge on Odlin Road. Closed September 6, 2016.

steps.title: A soda fountain in Wollaston
steps.text: Howard D. Johnson buys a store for $500 of borrowed money and makes his name with ice cream.

steps.title: Franchising carries the name out of state
steps.text: Orleans on Cape Cod in 1935, Milford, Connecticut in 1936. The operators pay for the buildings.

steps.title: The turnpike
steps.text: The company wins the contract for 24 restaurants on the Pennsylvania Turnpike.

steps.title: Times Square, and the last three open
steps.text: Lake George (1953) and Lake Placid (1956) are already trading when the Times Square restaurant opens. Bangor follows in 1966.

steps.title: The peak, and the sale
steps.text: 1,040 restaurants in 42 states pass to Imperial Group. The turnpike monopoly ends the same year.

steps.title: Eight left
steps.text: Times Square closes. The AP counts eight restaurants in six states.

steps.title: Bangor closes
steps.text: The motel stays open. Lake George is the last Howard Johnson’s restaurant.

steps.title: Lake George closes
steps.text: The last orange roof goes dark and the property is offered for lease.

blocks.body: Not shown: the roughly 1,000 other restaurants. We found no complete, dated location list in a source we could verify, and we did not want to plot pins from enthusiast sites we could not check.
